opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. What really excites me is that so much of human reasoning isn't purely verbal. When you're working through a geometry problem, planning furniture in a room, or figuring out how a mechanical part fits together, you sketch. You draw a diagram, look at it, notice something you didn't see before, and revise. The picture becomes part of the thinking, not just an input or an output.

For a long time, multimodal models treated images as something you either read at the start or generated at the end. The reasoning in between happened entirely in text. That's a real limitation, because some problems are much easier to solve visually. Describing a spatial arrangement in words can be clumsy and lossy, whereas a quick rendered image captures it directly.

So the idea of letting a model generate or edit images as intermediate steps, like a visual scratchpad, is really compelling to me. The model could draw an auxiliary line on a diagram, zoom into a region, mark up a map, or imagine what a scene looks like from another angle, and then use that to inform its next step. It's closer to how people actually think.

There's also an interesting feedback loop. If a model generates an image and then has to reason about it, it gets a chance to catch its own mistakes. If the picture doesn't look right, that tells you something about your understanding. I think that kind of grounded, self-checking visual reasoning could make models more reliable on tasks where text-only reasoning tends to hallucinate or lose track of spatial details.

And on the generation side, which is where a lot of my work has been, it flips things around. Thinking can help make better images. Instead of producing a picture in one shot, the model can plan, draft, critique, and refine. So for me it's really about breaking down the wall between understanding and generation and letting them improve each other.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes generating or editing images as intermediate visual scratchpad steps that inform the model’s next reasoning step.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so for me it comes down to the fact that a lot of reasoning just isn't linguistic. When you watch people solve a geometry problem, or figure out how a mechanism works, or even plan a route through a building, they're not narrating it to themselves in sentences. They're sketching, they're rotating things in their head, they're drawing an auxiliary line on the diagram and going, "oh, now I see it." Language is kind of a lossy serialization of that process.

And so when we train models to do all of their thinking as a chain of text tokens, we're forcing them to route every spatial or visual intuition through this bottleneck of describing it in words. Sometimes that works fine. But there are a lot of tasks where describing the picture is harder than just having the picture. Counting objects in a cluttered scene, understanding where things are relative to each other, checking whether a layout actually fits. The model ends up producing these long verbal descriptions that are sort of an approximation of what it would have been able to just look at.

What got me excited is this idea that the model could instead produce an intermediate visual artifact as part of its reasoning. Crop in on a region, draw a bounding box, mark up a diagram, render a candidate edit and then look at the result. The image becomes a scratchpad, the same way the text chain of thought is a scratchpad. And then it can go back and forth, text, image, text, image, and each modality is doing the part it's actually good at.

The other thing I'd say is that it makes the reasoning more legible. If the model draws the line it's reasoning about, I can see whether it's drawing the right line. That's a lot more useful to me as a person checking its work than a paragraph claiming it considered the right thing.

r001.rationale: The response says models can produce visual artifacts—such as markups or candidate edits—as a reasoning scratchpad and then inspect them, clearly communicating that image generation enables images to be part of reasoning.

astra-6.text:
What interests me is that images can be more than just inputs to a model. They can also be a way for the model to work through a problem. Humans do this all the time—we sketch something, draw a diagram, or imagine how an object would look from another angle. That representation helps us reason about things that would be awkward to describe entirely in words.

So the interesting question is: can a model do something similar? Can it create or manipulate a visual representation, look at the result, and use that to decide what to do next? For a spatial problem, for example, a drawing might make a relationship explicit that’s difficult to keep track of in text.

The key is whether that visual step actually helps the model solve the problem. Producing a plausible-looking image is one thing; using it as a useful intermediate step in reasoning is another. That’s the capability I find exciting.

r001.rationale: The response says a model could create or manipulate a visual representation, inspect it, and use it to decide what to do next—using generated images as an intermediate step in reasoning.

sol-6.1.text:
What interests me is that a lot of the things we reason about are fundamentally spatial or visual, and language can be a pretty indirect way to represent them. If you’re trying to understand how objects fit together, or what might happen if you move something in a scene, being able to work with an image could be really useful.

There’s also a distinction between looking at an image and using an image to think. Could a model sketch a possible solution, inspect that sketch, notice a problem, and revise it? We do that all the time with diagrams or drawings. I’m interested in whether that kind of process can help models solve problems that are difficult to work through entirely in words.

r001.rationale: The response describes a model sketching a possible solution, inspecting it, and revising it, presenting image generation as part of the model’s reasoning process.
